Q: Are there any builtin frozen modules in python A:

Thanks to the existing answer from @user2357112, here's a function I am using to detect frozen modules:

def get_frozen_modules():
    try:
        import _imp
        return _imp._frozen_module_names()
    except (ImportError, AttributeError):
        pass

    import ctypes as c
    class Frozen(c.Structure):
        _fields_ = ("name", c.c_char_p), ("code", c.c_void_p), ("size", c.c_int)

    modules = c.POINTER(Frozen).in_dll(c.pythonapi, "PyImport_FrozenModules")
    result = []
    for frozen in modules:
        if frozen.name is None:
            break
        result.append(frozen.name.decode("ascii"))
    return result

print(get_frozen_modules())

Tested in python 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, 3.15

As noted, the main shift occured in 3.11. But in this version the function _imp._frozen_module_names was introduced, it is used in the internal tooling, and most likely cointroduced by the preparation for hosting the import mechanism in python importlib/_bootstrap.py and is unlikely to go away, so using it is very convinient and kind of future proofs us. It hides all the private undocumented arrays and saves us from changing Frozen structure.

As for versions under 3.11 the frozen module layout is a bit different, it does not include is_package field. (Keeping this field creates issues reading the array). And there's only PyImport_FrozenModules to care about, so this simplifies our function.

If you are not targetting 3.1 or 3.2, you can remove ImportError check. The _imp module did not exist in those versions.

Also I am using c_void_p just to ensure alignment. We don't need the whole correct type ( POINTER(c_ubyte) ), since we are not accessing the field anyways.

Another cool thing is that the POINTER is actually iterable, we don't have to do the ugly data[i] manually!

Q: What are the differences between setattr and __set__? A:

Function setattr(object, name, value, /) can be called to set an arbitrary attribute specified by argument name of some instance specified by argument object to a some value specified by argument value. For example:

Function __set__ is a descriptor method. A descriptor is an object that is a class attribute and that controls access to an instance attribute. If, for example, the descriptor is assigned to a class attribute named x, then when there is an assignment to instance attribute x, the descriptor's __set__ method will be called:

# setattr example:
class Foo:
    pass

foo = Foo()
setattr(foo, 'x', 17)
print('foo.x =', foo.x)

#__set__ example:
class INT:
    """Only allow int values to be assigned."""
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        # name will be the name of the attribute being assigned
        self.name = name

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        if not isinstance(value, int):
            raise TypeError(f'Values assigned to attribute {self.name} must be of type int')
        # We cannot use a call to setattr as that would result in this method
        # being recursively called. Instead, we update the dictionary directly.
        # Note that this only works when the there is a dictionary:
        instance.__dict__[self.name] = value


class Bar:
    # Instance attribute x must be an int.
    x = INT()  # x.name will be 'x'


    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x  # x must be an int

bar = Bar(7)
bar.x = 9
print('bar.x =', bar.x)
bar.x = 's'  # This will raise an exception

Prints:

foo.x = 17
bar.x = 9
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "C:\Ron\test\test.py", line 37, in <module>
    bar.x = 's'  # This will raise an exception
    ^^^^^
  File "C:\Booboo\test\test.py", line 19, in __set__
    raise TypeError(f'Values assigned to attribute {self.name} must be of type int')
TypeError: Values assigned to attribute x must be of type int

The INT descriptor above will not work if the class does not use a dictionary for storing its attributes. To be able to use setattr, which makes no assumptions as to how instance attributes are stored, we must assign the value using a name other than the name of the attribute being managed. This will require us to also define a __get__ method so that we can retrieve the actual attribute value:

class INT:
    """Only allow int values to be assigned."""
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
        # name will be the name of the attribute being assigned
        self.name = name
        # The actual instance attribute name used to store the value:
        self.attribute_name = '_' + name

    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        if not isinstance(value, int):
            raise TypeError(f'Values assigned to attribute {self.name} must be of type int')
        setattr(instance, self.attribute_name, value)

    def __get__(self, instance, owner=None):
        return getattr(instance, self.attribute_name) if instance else self


class Bar:
    # Instance attribute x must be an int.
    x = INT()  # x.name will be 'x'


    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x  # x must be an int

bar = Bar(7)
bar.x = 9
print('bar.x =', bar.x)

Q: Non periodic square function train in python A:

The thing to do is to just write some custom code, instead of built-in modules like to tried. For instance:

from matplotlib import pyplot as plt

def plot_square_pulses(n, p, dur, amp, offset):
    plt.figure()
    for i in range(n):
        x1 = i * (p + dur) + offset
        x2 = x1 + dur
        plt.hlines(amp, x1, x2, linewidth=2)
        plt.vlines(x1, 0, amp, linewidth=2)
        plt.vlines(x2, 0, amp, linewidth=2)
    plt.axis('equal')

# Example usage:
plot_square_pulses(n=5, p=0.3, dur=1, amp=1, offset=0.2)
